Appropriate Methodology supporting text: The use of CNN for image classification is appropriate and standard for this type of computer vision task. The comparison against traditional ML techniques (SVM, NB) with feature extractors (HOG) provides a logical baseline to justify the deep learning approach.
Reproducibility supporting text: The authors provide the Python environment, some hyperparameters (lr=0.001, batch=50, epochs=100), and a high-level architectural description (17 layers, filter sizes). However, the custom dataset is not publicly available, and the specific layer configurations/feature map depths are incompletely defined, making exact replication impossible.
Dataset Adequately Described supporting: The dataset source (Shoolini University), size (264 images), capture device (Honor 6X), and labeling method (self-reported by students) are described. However, crucial details like the exact number of participants, age, gender split, and class distribution (Understanding vs. Not Understanding) are missing.
Appropriate Evaluation Metrics supportin: Accuracy, RMSE, and MAE are reported. However, for a small dataset with an unknown class balance, Accuracy alone is insufficient. Precision, Recall, and F1-score are critical to determine if the model is just predicting the majority class, especially given the suspiciously high "overall accuracy" of 98% compared to 92% test accuracy.
Comparison to Baselines / SOTA supportin: The paper compares its custom CNN against two traditional ML baselines (SVM, Naive Bayes) and proves its superiority. However, it does not compare against any contemporary State-of-the-Art FER or engagement detection deep learning models (e.g., ResNet, VGG, or existing engagement frameworks).
XAI Sufficiently Evaluated supporting te: No Explainable AI methods were implemented or evaluated in this study.
Limitations Explicitly Acknowledged supp: The authors implicitly acknowledge a dataset limitation by stating future work will "add more students images from different locations." However, they fail to acknowledge the severe methodological limitation of their dataset size (264 images is extremely small for deep learning) and the clear signs of overfitting (98% overall accuracy vs 92% test accuracy on a tiny dataset).
